case_studies.title: NeuroAgent: LLM Agents for Multimodal Neuroimaging Analysis and Research
case_studies.abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging analysis often involves complex, modality-specific preprocessing workflows that require careful configuration, quality control, and coordination across heterogeneous toolchains. Beyond preprocessing, downstream statistical analysis and disease classification commonly require task-specific code, evaluation protocols, and data-format conventions, creating additional barriers between raw acquisitions and reproducible scientific analysis. We present NeuroAgent, an LLM-driven agentic framework that automates key preprocessing and analysis steps for heterogeneous neuroimaging
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of complex neuroimaging analysis by building an automated framework called NeuroAgent. NeuroAgent automates key preprocessing and analysis steps for heterogeneous neuroimaging data. The result is a more streamlined and reproducible scientific analysis process.

case_studies.title: Algospeak, Hiding in the Open: The Trade-off Between Legible Meaning and Detection Avoidance
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate both content generation and moderation, linguistic evasion strategies known as Algospeak have intensified the coevolution between evaders and detectors. This research formalizes the underlying dynamics grounded in a joint action model: when Algospeak increases, detectability and understandability decrease. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of linguistic evasion strategies in large language models, introducing the concept of Majority Understandable Modulation, and finds that as evasion increases, detectability and understandability decrease. The authors built a joint action model to formalize the dynamics between evaders and detectors. The result shows a trade-off between hiding from detectors and being understood by recipients.

case_studies.title: Cited but Not Verified: Parsing and Evaluating Source Attribution in LLM Deep Research Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) power deep research agents that synthesize information from hundreds of web sources into cited reports, yet these citations cannot be reliably verified. Current approaches either trust models to self-cite accurately, risking bias, or employ retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that does not validate source accessibility, relevance, or factual consistency. We introduce the first source attribution evaluation framework that uses a reproducible AST parser to extract and evaluate inline citations from LLM-generated Markdown reports at scale. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable source citation in large language models by introducing a framework to evaluate and verify source attribution in generated reports. The researchers built a source attribution evaluation framework that uses a reproducible parser to extract and evaluate inline citations. The result is a more reliable way to validate source accessibility, relevance, and factual consistency in LLM-generated reports.

case_studies.title: TSCG: Deterministic Tool-Schema Compilation for Agentic LLM Deployments
case_studies.abstract: Production agent frameworks (OpenAI Function Calling, Anthropic Tool Use, MCP) transmit tool schemas as JSON, a format designed for machine parsing, not for interpretation by language models. For small models (4B-14B), this protocol mismatch accounts for the majority of tool-use failure at production catalog sizes. We present TSCG, a deterministic tool-schema compiler that resolves this mismatch at the API boundary, converting JSON schemas into token-efficient structured text without model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of tool-schema compilation for large language models, by building a deterministic tool-schema compiler called TSCG, which converts JSON schemas into structured text, resulting in improved tool-use success rates. TSCG resolves the protocol mismatch between production agent frameworks and language models. This research is relevant to IT engineers managing AI and machine learning infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Authorization Propagation in Multi-Agent AI Systems: Identity Governance as Infrastructure
case_studies.abstract: The security discussion around agentic AI focuses heavily on prompt injection. This paper argues that multi-agent systems also create a distinct authorization problem: maintaining authorization invariants as non-human principals retrieve data, delegate tasks, and synthesize results across changing boundaries. We call this problem authorization propagation. It is not reducible to prompt injection and is not fully addressed by classical access-control models such as RBAC, ABAC, or ReBAC. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of authorization propagation in multi-agent AI systems, where non-human principals access and share data across changing boundaries. The authors built a framework to formalize authorization propagation as a workflow-level property. The result is a new approach to identity governance in AI systems.

case_studies.title: When and Why SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Theoretical Study Based on $\ell_1$-norm Lower Bounds
case_studies.abstract: Sign-based optimization algorithms, such as SignSGD and Muon, have garnered significant attention for their remarkable performance in training large foundation models. Despite this empirical success, we still lack a theoretical understanding of when and why these sign-based methods outperform vanilla SGD.
